sections.title: The same modality isn't the same everywhere
It's not a lack of wanting

toc.title: Part three: safety can bring up defensive feelings

sections.title: Why the old defense comes up

blocks.p: I want to talk about having tried everything, about shutdown and numbness, and about how safety can actually lead to defensive feelings. My hope is that you gain some clarity into what's keeping you stuck, and some new ideas for getting a bit more unstuck, starting now.
A while back, one listener sent me this message:

q: I've been working with a trauma specialist therapist once a week, and we've been doing EMDR. I'm on Zoloft, which I started back in February, which has been the only thing to help me basically be able to function again.

I am diagnosed with C-PTSD from childhood misattunement, basically. I have really no connection with feelings. I don't have DID, but I just don't feel connected anymore. Whenever I feel into my body, I never feel safety. ... At this point I am skeptical about anything being able to help me.

I assume I'm stuck at the way bottom of the polyvagal ladder and just feel like I haven't budged up at all. I know someone probably thinks that they are the worst case scenario, but I swear I am. I've literally tried everything. When I try to feel safety in my body, all I feel is anxiousness rolling around in my tummy every time.
I can't seem to get past it. Hopefully, you maybe have experienced this before.

blocks.p: I'll take it in three parts: "I've tried everything," then shutdown and numbness, then why safety can bring up defensive feelings.
This might not be an issue of technique. It may not be an issue of ideas. It may be more an issue of implementation.

Say "I've tried everything" includes "I've tried meditating." Okay. What meditation looks like for you is not necessarily what it looks like for the next person. How it's taught and how it's implemented might be different from person to person, or guru to guru. What I think about meditation might not match the next person's.

So when we say "I've tried everything," my question is: what did it look like for you? Was that technique, or the way you did it, the right fit for you? Not just for you, but for the state you were in, because it may not have been.

I'm talking in general now, for all of us. We have to find what works for us. No matter what the technique or therapeutic modality is, it has to be the right fit for us, and it has to be done in a way that feels safe enough. If you're attempting meditation and it doesn't feel safe, it's not going to help. Or at least the way you're doing it isn't going to help. There might be a way that's a better fit for you, but that's something you have to explore.

For me, I don't like prerecorded guided meditations. That doesn't do it for me. All of a sudden the person is talking about light beams channeling through me, and I'm like, "No, there aren't. There are no light beams. It's just me." I need something that's in the moment. I like my own self-guided thing. I get the idea of what I want out of meditation, and when I attempt it, I'm good. I don't need someone telling me there are light beams.

The point is, it has to work for you. I don't know the right answer for you. I don't know the right answer for any of us. I don't know which technique is best for you. What I do know is that it's extremely important to build the capacity to feel safe. There are things that bring many of us to safety, like music, sensory stimulation, and movement. What that looks like for you, I don't know, and that's completely honest. You have to bring some curiosity to it.

So as you're reading up on different Instagram therapists and guru people, take what they're saying, that's fine, but ask yourself: "Is this right for me? Is this right for me right now, in the state I'm in, in this moment?" It might not be.

blocks.h3: The same modality isn't the same everywhere

blocks.p: You'd think therapy modalities work like a medical model: here's the diagnosis, and here's the modality, which is like a medicine or a tool or a technique that will remedy the diagnosis. But that's not true. Even the same therapy modality will be more or less effective based on who is implementing it. How I do somatic work, and how I integrate it into my therapeutic stance, is going to be different from the next person who also does somatic work.

I'm not trained in EMDR, and I don't know enough about it to speak on any expert level. But I've heard an EMDR therapist say, "What I do in EMDR does not match what I'm hearing from other people." And I've had at least one client tell me that their previous EMDR therapist jumped straight to the bilateral stimulation in session one. I know there's a lot more to EMDR than moving your eyes back and forth, and I don't think that's the right way to do it. But don't quote me on that.

The point is that fidelity to the model isn't guaranteed. These models are built to flow a certain way, more or less. I've been on treatment teams where my fellow therapists discussed which modalities they used. I'd spent time with these people. I'd shadowed sessions when I was brand new to the field. I'd seen them work. And what they named and labeled as their modality did not match what I'd seen. I was kind of like, "Oh, you call that CBT? Okay then."

So we might say, "I've tried everything. I've tried EMDR, CBT, DBT, ACT, all the letters of the alphabet in every possible order, and nothing works." I get it. But was it given with fidelity? Was it given by someone you actually had a connection with? Was it the right technique for you, in that moment, on that day? It's hard to say you've tried everything. I don't think anyone means that literally, although I think this listener did.
So what I'd ask each of us to ask ourselves is: what do I need in this moment, based on the state I'm in? EMDR might not be it. CBT might not be it. Ask yourself:

ul: What do I need for my system right now?
Maybe, what would feel challenging that I can tolerate?

blocks.p: Then try things based on your state. If you're in a shutdown state, going boxing may not be helpful. If you're in therapy, your therapist needs to be able to read what state you're in, and to adapt their techniques to it.
I get it. We feel like we've tried everything. We might be at a place of feeling hopeless or helpless. But I don't think the options are done.
Shutdown and a lack of feeling go together. Shutdown and numbness go together.

Shutdown is a dorsal vagal response, and it's all about conservation. The body is conserving resources to prepare for a potential escape. It's still neurocepting for the potential to escape the situation, but it's also kind of preparing for death, in a way.

Numbness is a big part of this. The body goes into actual physical numbness, or even dissociation. And it's not just the body. On more of a day-to-day level, the person who's stuck in shutdown feels emotionally numb. They feel empty. They feel hopeless. They say things like, "Nothing will help."

This is absolutely at the bottom of the ladder. It's the last option, the last autonomic shift for a mammal to potentially survive whatever situation it's in. If it can't be safe, if it can't run away, if it can't fight, then it will shut down and go into this conservation, collapse state. That's different from freeze.

In my opinion, shutdown might be the most difficult state to climb out of. It's way at the bottom, so maybe that's part of it. But a lot comes along with it. There's a lack of energy, and letting that energy return to the system is not easy. Doing it by yourself is not easy. Co-regulation can be very helpful.
Deb Dana said this when she was on the podcast:

q: In the beginning, for many people, climbing out of dorsal is really difficult... They need a co-regulator. They need somebody to accompany them.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h3: It's not a lack of wanting

blocks.p: The person in shutdown feels and reports being very defeated. There's a lack of motivation that comes along with it. Not because they're not trying. That's not the issue. They lack the energy to be motivated.

Somebody stuck in shutdown wants things to be different. They don't want to be shut down. They don't want to lack motivation or feel empty. It's not an issue of want. They simply lack the energy. Their body is in a conservation state, and everything slows down.

Coming out of shutdown, they have to learn all over again, or maybe for the first time, about pretty much everything: what it feels like to be safe, to have energy, to have aggression in a healthy way, to feel anxiety and be able to deal with it, to trust and connect with people. Maybe you're coming back to these things. Or maybe they're flat out brand new.
That's especially true with C-PTSD, complex post-traumatic stress disorder. I'd argue that shutdown is a major piece of C-PTSD.

With C-PTSD, there's a lack of a history of connection and safety. So feeling those things, and climbing out of shutdown, is a tall order. The person probably had a lack of healthy play, which is so important for kids. They may have lacked a healthy attachment, which is extremely important for kids. And if that's true, they lacked co-regulation, which means they lacked safety cues coming from a safe adult in their life.

So this person is going to end up in more of a shutdown state. Not having a safe attachment isn't something you can run away from or fight. If you're unable to connect to safe others, you end up in a more collapsed, withdrawn, isolated dorsal vagal response over time.

If you don't get those needs met, you may never really develop a truer self. I don't know what "true self" means, so I'll say truer: an accurate understanding of who you are, how you are, how you feel, what safety feels like. A greater range of experiences and feelings and emotions. An understanding of your somatic self, what emotions feel like in your body.

All of this is built on a history of co-regulation, and if you don't have that, your self-development is compromised. We learn who we are in the context of others. We build off of a safe attachment. We build off of co-regulation. I don't think we enter the world as just who we are. We build off of what we're given, and hopefully we're given a solid foundation of love, connection, and encouragement, along with challenge we can meet and grow from, so we feel successful and confident. That's just a smattering of what I think is important for developing a sense of who we are, how we are, and what we're capable of.
If you don't get that, you're probably going to end up in more of a shutdown state. So feeling connection and trust and love and hope and motivation is hard. Not impossible, but hard.

blocks.h: Part three: safety can bring up defensive feelings

blocks.p: This might seem odd, but safety can actually lead to defensive feelings.

Your autonomic nervous system is constantly detecting for safety or danger. I'm not trying to personify it or give it agency, but there's an inner drive to self-regulate. The ideal state for the autonomic nervous system is the self-regulated state, which leads to greater health, growth, and restoration. So it's searching for safe environments and safe people in our lives.

When it's in those safe environments, or with those safe people, it may begin the process of self-regulation, or of receiving co-regulation from a safe other. And along with that regulation may come some defensive feelings.

This listener mentioned meditation, but the same would be true for yoga, or even therapy. Whenever you bring more mindfulness, you're bringing the focus of your consciousness to yourself and your true, or close to true, experience in the present moment.

Mindfulness is like aligning your consciousness with your body. You're bringing your focus to the physical self. That's the way I frame it in my mind: mindfulness gives your autonomic nervous system permission to self-regulate. If you're focused on the outside world, or even on thoughts about your internal world, you're not focused on your body. Once you bring awareness to your body, the two are in alignment, and self-regulation can begin to happen.

Animals don't have that problem. They don't think about the outside world and dwell on it. They're always in tune with their inner body, so they're always in a state of self-regulation, and also offering co-regulation to each other.

In meditation, you're probably in a safe environment, maybe even with safe people. When I meditate, I like the lights down. I like low stimulation. Those are cues to my autonomic nervous system that we're in safety. I do better with low stimulation. As it neuroceps safety, the potential for self-regulation increases.

So part of meditation is the mindfulness, and part of it is the environment: giving yourself cues of safety. Increasing environmental safety cues is so important. When I teach building safety, it's the first lesson.

blocks.h3: Why the old defense comes up

blocks.p: When we give ourselves environmental safety cues, or co-regulation with safe others, or just mindfully look inward, self-regulation starts. And along with it come defensive feelings as we climb our polyvagal ladder.

It's interesting, maybe kind of weird, that as we feel more safety, some of that defensive stuff comes up, even some of the old defensive stuff. So it's actually kind of a good thing, if you can tolerate it. This could happen in therapy too. It really comes down to: can you tolerate it?

You have to have the window of tolerance, or the vagal brake, developed enough to tolerate the defensive feelings that are going to come up. Once you do, they won't be felt as defense. They'll be felt as something else. Instead of coming out of shutdown and up into a fight state and feeling anger, it won't feel like anger. It'll feel like power. It's a much different experience.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: So we have to strengthen the window of tolerance, the vagal brake. You can do that by finding what brings you to safety and developing it, spending more time doing those things mindfully. I'd encourage you to feel safety in tolerable doses, little by little.

It's like lifting weights. You're not going to lift 100 pounds before you lift 75, and you can't lift 75 before you can lift 50. Similarly, you won't be able to experience joy until you can experience a little joy. The more you can build those safety feelings in doses, the more you increase your capacity to feel more of them.
You're exercising the biological pathways, the ventral vagal pathways, so you can increase the potential and the longevity of feeling and staying in your safety state.
